explanation: Standing wave ratio (SWR) is a measure of how well a load — the antenna system — is matched to the characteristic impedance of the transmission line feeding it: a perfect match gives 1:1 SWR, and increasing mismatch raises the ratio along with the fraction of power reflected back toward the transmitter instead of being radiated. SWR has nothing to do with an amplifier's power output-to-input ratio (that's gain or efficiency, a separate spec), transmitter efficiency in general, or the quality of a station's ground connection — none of those are what an SWR meter measures.

question: Which of the following is a safety hazard of a 12-volt storage battery that lacks internal protection circuitry?
answers: Touching both terminals with your hands can cause electrical shock
Shorting the terminals can cause burns, fire, or an explosion
RF emissions from a nearby transmitter can cause the electrolyte to emit poison gas
explanation: A 12V lead-acid or SLA cell has very low internal resistance, so a dead short across the terminals can drive tens to hundreds of amps through the fault. Without a fuse, PTC, or BMS to interrupt that current, the energy dissipates as heat right at the short — enough to melt metal, ignite nearby material, or build gas pressure fast enough to rupture the case. Touching both terminals with dry skin at 12V typically can't push a hazardous shock current through the body, and RF from a nearby transmitter has nothing to do with electrolyte off-gassing, so those distractors describe hazards that don't really apply to a bare 12V battery.

question: What health hazard is posed by electrical current flowing through the body?
answers: It may cause injury by heating body tissue
It may disrupt the electrical functions of cells
It may cause involuntary muscle contractions
explanation: Current through the body can injure by three separate mechanisms: resistive (I²R) heating of tissue, disruption of the body's own electrical signaling (most dangerously, throwing the heart into ventricular fibrillation or interfering with nerve conduction), and involuntary muscle contraction (the 'can't let go' effect, or being thrown from the source). All three are real, independent shock-injury pathways, which is why the exam's synthesis answer is correct rather than any single mechanism alone.

question: In the United States, what circuit does black wire insulation indicate in a three-wire 120 V AC cable?
explanation: Under the standard US NEC wiring color code for 120V branch circuits, black insulation marks the ungrounded (hot) conductor, white marks the grounded (neutral) conductor, and green or bare copper marks the equipment grounding conductor. 'Negative' isn't a meaningful label here — that's DC terminology, and household branch wiring is AC, which has no fixed polarity.

question: What is the purpose of a fuse in an electrical circuit?
answers: To prevent power supply ripple from damaging a component
To remove power in case of an overload
To limit current and prevent shocks
explanation: A fuse's job is simple: its element melts open when current exceeds its rated value long enough, removing power from the circuit before an overload or fault overheats the wiring or the load. It doesn't smooth or filter power-supply ripple (that's a capacitor/regulator job) and it doesn't gently 'limit' current or protect a person from shock the way a GFCI does — it's a one-shot overcurrent disconnect, not a current regulator.

question: Why should a 5-ampere fuse never be replaced with a 20-ampere fuse?
answers: The larger fuse would be likely to blow because it is rated for higher current
The power supply ripple would greatly increase
Excessive current could cause a fire
Voltage drop in the higher current fuse could result in excessively low voltage to the device
explanation: The wiring and components downstream of a 5A fuse are sized on the assumption that fault current will be interrupted at 5A. Swapping in a 20A fuse lets four times that current flow before anything opens, which can overheat conductors and components well past the point the original fuse was protecting against — a real fire risk. It has nothing to do with the bigger fuse blowing more easily (a higher-rated fuse is actually harder to blow) or with ripple/voltage drop, which fuses don't meaningfully affect.

question: What is a good way to guard against electrical shock at your station?
answers: Use three-wire cords and plugs for all AC powered equipment
Connect all AC powered station equipment to a common safety ground
Ensure all capacitors used for high-voltage DC are fully discharged before working inside equipment
explanation: All three practices are standard station wiring safety: three-wire cords/plugs ground every chassis to the safety ground pin, bonding all AC-powered station equipment to one common safety ground keeps every enclosure at the same potential (so touching two pieces of gear at once can't shock you), and discharging high-voltage capacitors before opening equipment removes stored charge that can remain lethal long after the supply is switched off. None of these substitutes for the others, which is why 'all these choices' is correct.

question: Where should a lightning arrester be installed in a coaxial feed line?
answers: At the output connector of a transceiver
At the AC power service panel
On a grounded panel near where feed lines enter the building
explanation: A coax lightning arrester belongs on a grounded bulkhead panel at the point where feed lines enter the building, bonded to the station's single-point ground system. That gives a lightning surge on the shield the shortest possible path to earth before it can travel further into the structure. Putting it at the antenna feed point or the transceiver's output connector leaves the run of coax (and the building) exposed to the surge, and the AC service panel is for protecting the power wiring, not the antenna feed line.

question: Where should a fuse or circuit breaker be installed in a 120V AC power circuit?
answers: In series with the hot conductor only
In series with the hot and neutral conductors
In parallel with the hot conductor only
In parallel with the hot and neutral conductors
explanation: A fuse or breaker for a 120V circuit must be in series with the hot conductor only. Opening the hot leg fully de-energizes the load; if instead the neutral (or both conductors) were the one protected, a fault could leave the load's internal wiring still connected to the hot conductor even after the neutral opened — live but appearing dead, a serious shock and fire hazard. A fuse wired in parallel wouldn't interrupt anything at all; it would just sit there as a dead-end bypass path.

question: What should be done to all external ground rods or earth connections?
answers: Waterproof them with silicone caulk or electrical tape
Keep them as far apart as possible
Bond them together with heavy wire or conductive strap
Tune them for resonance on the lowest frequency of operation
explanation: Separate grounds (AC service ground, tower ground, station equipment ground) that aren't bonded together can sit at very different potentials relative to each other during a lightning strike or fault, because each has different impedance to a strike or surge some distance away. That potential difference is exactly what arcs across equipment or through a person standing between two 'grounds.' Bonding every ground rod together with heavy wire or strap (per standard NEC Article 250/810 bonding practice) forces the whole system to rise and fall together, eliminating that difference. Waterproofing, spacing grounds apart, or 'tuning' them for resonance are not real or correct practices.

question: What hazard exists when rapidly charging or discharging an unprotected battery?
explanation: Pushing high current into or out of a cell faster than its chemistry and construction can dissipate the resulting heat causes internal temperature (and in some chemistries, internal gas pressure from side reactions) to climb quickly. Without a protection circuit to cap the current, there's nothing to stop that from running away into overheating, venting, or worse. Ripple and overvoltage are power-supply concerns rather than the core battery-abuse hazard here, and a 12V cell isn't primarily a shock hazard through skin contact.

question: What hazard exists in a power supply immediately after turning it off?
answers: Circulating currents in the dc filter
Leakage flux in the power transformer
explanation: The large electrolytic filter capacitors in a power supply store charge and can hold a lethal voltage for seconds to minutes after the supply is switched off and unplugged — especially in higher-voltage supplies like tube-type HV finals. That's why technicians verify zero voltage with a meter (or rely on bleeder resistors) before opening a supply chassis, rather than trusting that 'off' means safe.

question: Which of the following precautions should be taken when measuring high voltages with a voltmeter?
answers: Ensure that the voltmeter has very low impedance
Ensure that the voltmeter and its leads are rated for use at the voltages being measured
Ensure that the circuit is grounded through the voltmeter
Ensure that the voltmeter is set to the correct frequency
explanation: Test leads and meters carry their own maximum working-voltage and CAT insulation rating; pushing them beyond that rating risks insulation breakdown, arc flash, or a meter that fails violently under a high-voltage fault. Before probing a high-voltage circuit, confirm both the meter and its leads are rated for the voltage you're about to measure. A low-impedance meter would load down the circuit and give a false reading (voltmeters are deliberately high-impedance), grounding the circuit through the meter is dangerous and pointless, and voltmeters don't have a 'frequency setting.'

question: Which of the following is good practice when installing ground wires on a tower for lightning protection?
answers: Put a drip loop in the ground connection to prevent water damage to the ground system
Make sure all ground wire bends are right angles
Ensure that connections are short and direct
explanation: Lightning surges are extremely fast, high di/dt pulses, and every extra foot of wire or sharp bend in a ground conductor adds inductance, which raises the voltage drop across that wire during a strike (V = L·di/dt) and can push the surge to flash over somewhere else instead of following the ground path to earth. Keeping ground wire runs short and direct minimizes that inductance. A drip loop or right-angle bends work against this goal rather than helping it.

question: What is required when climbing an antenna tower?
answers: Have sufficient training on safe tower climbing techniques
Use appropriate tie-off to the tower at all times
Always wear an approved climbing harness
explanation: Tower climbing safety, consistent with standard fall-protection practice (the kind codified in OSHA fall-protection rules and ANSI/ASSE Z359 as applied to tower work), requires all three: proper training in climbing technique, continuous tie-off to the tower, and wearing an approved climbing harness at all times. Skipping any one of these removes a layer of fall protection, so the complete answer is that all three are required.

question: Under what circumstances is it safe to climb a tower without a helper or observer?
answers: When no electrical work is being performed
When no mechanical work is being performed
When the work being done is not more than 20 feet above the ground
explanation: The correct answer is never. A ground-level helper or observer is there to call for emergency help, assist with a gin pole or rope, or spot hazards like traffic and nearby power lines. That safety function doesn't go away just because the work is 'only' mechanical, 'only' electrical, or close to the ground — a fall or medical emergency with no one aware of it can be fatal regardless of height or task.

question: Which of the following is an important safety precaution to observe when putting up an antenna tower?
answers: Wear a ground strap connected to your wrist at all times
Insulate the base of the tower to avoid lightning strikes
Look for and stay clear of any overhead electrical wires
explanation: Contact between a tower, an antenna, or a mast section and an overhead power line during installation is one of the leading causes of fatal accidents in amateur tower work, so watching for and staying clear of any overhead electrical wires is critical before and during the raise. This has nothing to do with wearing a wrist ground strap (that's ESD protection for bench electronics, not personal safety on a tower) or insulating the tower base, which isn't standard or effective lightning practice.

question: What is the purpose of a safety wire through a turnbuckle used to tension guy lines?
answers: Secure the guy line if the turnbuckle breaks
Prevent loosening of the turnbuckle from vibration
Provide a ground path for lightning strikes
Provide an ability to measure for proper tensioning
explanation: A turnbuckle is threaded, and wind-driven vibration and repeated load cycling on a guy line can slowly back the barrel off its threads over time, loosening the guy. A safety wire (or cotter pin) run through the turnbuckle mechanically locks it against that rotation so it can't work loose. It isn't a backup structural connection if the turnbuckle itself fails, it doesn't provide a lightning ground path, and it has no role in measuring tension.

question: What is the minimum safe distance from a power line to allow when installing an antenna?
answers: Add the height of the antenna to the height of the power line and multiply by a factor of 1.5
The height of the power line above ground
Enough so that if the antenna falls, no part of it can come within 10 feet of the power wires
explanation: The standard rule of thumb is to plan for the worst case: site and size the installation so that if the antenna and its mast were to fall over, no part of it could come within 10 feet of the power wires. That's a fall-radius calculation based on the antenna structure itself, not a formula tied to the power line's own height or to a wavelength at the operating frequency, which have no bearing on physical clearance from energized conductors.

question: Which of the following is an important safety rule to remember when using a crank-up tower?
answers: This type of tower must never be painted
This type of tower must never be grounded
This type of tower must not be climbed unless it is retracted, or mechanical safety locking devices have been installed
explanation: A crank-up (telescoping) tower is held extended mainly by its cable-and-winch system. If that cable slips, breaks, or is bumped while someone is on an extended, unlocked tower, the sections can telescope down suddenly and crush or shear anything in the way. The safety rule is that a crank-up tower must not be climbed unless it's fully retracted or mechanical safety locking pins have been installed to positively hold each section, removing that collapse hazard before anyone goes up.

question: Which is a proper grounding method for a tower?
answers: A single four-foot ground rod, driven into the ground no more than 12 inches from the base
A ferrite-core RF choke connected between the tower and ground
A connection between the tower base and a cold-water pipe
Separate eight-foot ground rods for each tower leg, bonded to the tower and each other
explanation: Good tower grounding practice (following NEC-based and commercial lightning-protection guidance) is a separate ground rod, typically at least 8 feet long, driven at each leg of the tower, with all the rods bonded to the tower base and to each other. Multiple bonded rods lower the overall ground system impedance and give a lightning strike several parallel paths to earth. A single rod close to the base, an RF choke in the ground path, or tying to a cold-water pipe are all inadequate substitutes that don't provide a real low-impedance path for a lightning surge.

question: Why should you avoid attaching an antenna to a utility pole?
answers: The antenna will not work properly because of induced voltages
The antenna may unbalance the power transformer, causing power fluctuations
The antenna could contact high-voltage power lines
explanation: Utility poles carry (or run close to) primary distribution voltages, so anything mounted on one — an antenna, a mast, or a person working on it — carries an elevated risk of contacting or arcing across to those energized conductors, on top of the fact that the pole belongs to the utility, not the ham. It isn't about induced voltages disabling the antenna's performance, and power transformers don't get 'unbalanced' by a nearby antenna.

question: Which of the following is true when installing grounding conductors used for lightning protection?
answers: Wires must be carefully routed with precise right-angle bends
explanation: Same physics as the ground-wire routing question above: a sharp bend in a lightning ground conductor acts like added inductance and a likely flashover point where a fast transient can jump to a nearby object instead of following the bend to earth. Straight, gently-routed runs are correct; precise right-angle bends are exactly what to avoid, insulated wire isn't a requirement, and bonding grounds together (a 'common ground') is the goal, not something to avoid.

question: Which of the following establishes grounding requirements for an amateur radio tower or antenna?
explanation: FCC Part 97 licenses and regulates amateur radio operation, but it doesn't set physical grounding or lightning-protection construction standards for towers and antennas. That's governed by the National Electrical Code as adopted and enforced through local electrical/building codes and inspectors. FAA rules in this context cover obstruction lighting and marking, not grounding, and UL 'recommended practices' aren't a legally enforceable code.

question: What type of radiation are radio signals?
explanation: Radio-frequency signals are non-ionizing radiation. Ionizing radiation (gamma rays, x-rays, alpha particles) carries enough energy per photon or particle to strip electrons from atoms and break chemical bonds outright; RF photons carry far too little energy per photon to do that. RF's hazard mechanism at legal exposure levels is thermal (tissue heating), not ionization.

question: Which of the following bands has the lowest maximum permissible exposure for RF safety?
explanation: FCC RF exposure limits under 47 CFR 1.1310 are most restrictive roughly in the 30–300 MHz range because that band straddles the whole-body resonant absorption frequency for an average standing adult (around 60–80 MHz depending on height and grounding) — the body simply absorbs RF energy most efficiently there, so the permitted power density is lowest. Among these choices, 50 MHz falls in that most-restrictive window, while 3.5 MHz (well below 30 MHz) and 440/1296 MHz (above 300 MHz) both have higher allowed power density limits.

question: How does the allowable power density for RF safety change if duty cycle changes from 100 percent to 50 percent?
answers: It increases by a factor of 3
It increases by a factor of 2
There is no adjustment allowed for lower duty cycle
explanation: MPE limits are defined against average power over the exposure averaging time. If a signal is transmitting only half the time (50% duty cycle) instead of continuously (100%), its time-averaged power at any given instantaneous power level is half of what a 100%-duty signal would produce. So to reach the same average exposure, you're allowed to run twice the instantaneous/peak power density at 50% duty cycle as at 100% duty cycle — the allowable power density increases by a factor of 2.

question: What factors affect the RF exposure of people near an amateur station antenna?
answers: Frequency and power level of the RF field
Distance from the antenna to a person
explanation: RF exposure at a given point is essentially a power-density calculation, and all three listed factors feed directly into it: the transmitter's power and frequency (which determine how much energy is radiated and how efficiently the antenna radiates it), the distance from the antenna (power density falls off with distance), and the antenna's radiation pattern (exposure is much higher in the main lobe than off to the side or behind the antenna). All three matter to a real RF exposure evaluation, so 'all these choices' is correct.

question: Why do exposure limits vary with frequency?
answers: Lower frequency RF fields have more energy than higher frequency fields
Lower frequency RF fields do not penetrate the human body
Higher frequency RF fields are transient in nature
The human body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others
explanation: Exposure limits vary with frequency because the human body doesn't absorb RF energy uniformly across the spectrum — absorption peaks near the body's resonant frequencies (roughly 30–300 MHz, as in T0C02) and is lower well above or below that range. It isn't that low-frequency fields carry more energy (photon energy actually rises with frequency, though negligibly at RF) or fail to penetrate the body, and 'transient' isn't a meaningful property of continuous RF fields.

question: Which of the following is an acceptable method to determine whether your station complies with FCC RF exposure regulations?
answers: By calculation based on FCC OET Bulletin 65
By calculation based on computer modeling
By measurement of field strength using calibrated equipment
explanation: The FCC accepts any of these as a valid way to demonstrate compliance with the 1.1310 exposure limits under the licensee-evaluation duty in 97.13(c): hand calculation using the standard methodology in OET Bulletin 65 (and its amateur-specific Supplement B), computer modeling software that implements the same underlying physics, or direct measurement of field strength with properly calibrated equipment. None of these is the sole 'official' method, which is why 'all these choices' is correct.

question: What hazard is created by touching an antenna during a transmission?
explanation: Touching an energized antenna produces an RF burn: current concentrates at the small contact point where skin resistance is relatively high, producing localized I²R heating similar to a contact burn, rather than the current-through-the-body mechanism of a 60 Hz electrocution. It also isn't ionizing-radiation exposure, since RF is non-ionizing (T0C01) — the hazard here is purely thermal at the point of contact.

question: Which of the following actions can reduce exposure to RF radiation?
explanation: Relocating the antennas — moving them farther from occupied areas, higher up, or reorienting the main beam away from people — directly reduces the power density people are exposed to, since exposure depends on distance from the radiating element and position in its pattern. Relocating just the transmitter (the radio itself) doesn't change anything about the field radiated at the antenna, and increasing duty cycle raises average exposure rather than reducing it — the opposite of what's being asked.

question: How can you make sure your station stays in compliance with RF safety regulations?
answers: By informing the FCC of any changes made in your station
By re-evaluating the station whenever an item in the transmitter or antenna system is changed
By making sure your antennas have low SWR
By using only Underwriter Laboratories approved transmitting equipment
explanation: Because RF exposure depends on transmitter power, frequency, antenna gain, pattern, height, and location, any change to those elements can push a previously-compliant station out of compliance with the 1.1310 limits. Under 97.13(c) the licensee's obligation is to re-evaluate the station whenever the transmitter or antenna system changes — there's no requirement to notify the FCC of routine station changes, low SWR only reflects transmitter/feed line efficiency (not the actual field strength people are exposed to), and there's no 'UL-approved transmitter' safe harbor in Part 97.

question: Why is duty cycle one of the factors used to determine safe RF radiation exposure levels?
answers: It affects the average exposure to radiation
It affects the peak exposure to radiation
It takes into account the antenna feed line loss
It takes into account the thermal effects of the final amplifier
explanation: The MPE limits (and their associated averaging times of 6 minutes for occupational/controlled exposure and 30 minutes for general population/uncontrolled exposure, per 1.1310) are defined in terms of average power over that window. A transmitter that's only actually keyed part of the time deposits proportionally less average RF energy into nearby tissue than one transmitting continuously at the same power, which is exactly why duty cycle factors into the exposure calculation — it affects the average, not the peak, exposure.

question: What is the definition of duty cycle during the averaging time for RF exposure?
answers: The difference between the lowest and highest power output of a transmitter
The difference between the PEP and the average power output of a transmitter
The percentage of time that a transmitter is transmitting
The percentage of time that a transmitter is not transmitting
explanation: For RF exposure purposes, duty cycle is defined as the percentage of time the transmitter is actually transmitting during the averaging period. A voice/SSB QSO with normal back-and-forth pauses might run well under 50% duty cycle, while a repeater or link keyed continuously approaches 100% — it's purely a measure of on-time, not a difference between power levels or PEP versus average power.

question: How does RF radiation differ from ionizing radiation (radioactivity)?
answers: RF radiation does not have sufficient energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA
RF radiation can only be detected with an RF dosimeter
RF radiation is limited in range to a few feet
explanation: RF radiation lacks the photon energy needed to directly break chemical bonds or damage DNA the way ionizing radiation (x-rays, gamma rays, energetic particles) can; at legal amateur power levels its biological effect is essentially thermal (tissue heating), not molecular damage. That doesn't make RF 'perfectly safe' — excessive exposure causes real thermal injury, which is exactly why exposure limits exist — and RF isn't limited in range to a few feet or measured with some special-purpose 'RF dosimeter'; ordinary calibrated field-strength instruments do the job.

question: Who is responsible for ensuring that no person is exposed to RF energy above the FCC exposure limits?
answers: Anyone who is near an antenna
explanation: Under 97.13(c), the personal, non-delegable responsibility for keeping RF exposure to any person below the FCC's 1.1310 limits rests with the station licensee. The FCC sets and enforces the limits but doesn't perform the per-station evaluation itself, and there's no equivalent compliance role for a bystander or a local zoning board — zoning addresses things like tower height and setbacks, not RF exposure compliance.
